principle_text: When the seller confirms the item's condition and usage history, avoid failing to address pricing to maintain negotiation leverage.
When the seller admits to slight skuff marks on the back of the item, you should leverage this information to negotiate a lower price based on the perceived wear and tear.

When the seller agrees to a price slightly below their initial asking price, you should offer additional conveniences or benefits, such as immediate pickup, to strengthen your negotiation position and achieve a better deal.
When the seller has already agreed on a price, avoid accepting the same price without attempting to negotiate further for a better deal.
When the seller shows interest in a trade-in offer and asks for more details, you should consider leveraging this opportunity to negotiate a lower price effectively.

When the seller emphasizes the item's condition without discussing price, avoid responding with polite greetings that do not address negotiation terms or pressure the seller to lower their initial price.
When the buyer references cheaper alternatives and proposes a lower price, you should consider accepting the offer to secure the deal and maintain a competitive edge in the negotiation.

When the seller suggests getting a refurbished unit instead of repairing a damaged item, avoid shifting the conversation towards non-essential items like external mice, as it may weaken your leverage in price negotiation.

When the seller mentions a higher reference price for refurbished items but expresses willingness to negotiate, you should inquire about the price to leverage the suggested starting point for further negotiation.

When the seller acknowledges a beat-up item and the buyer offers a lower price for a less aesthetically pleasing product, the buyer should emphasize willingness to accept a lower-quality item to negotiate a better deal.
When the seller confirms the product's good condition without addressing price negotiation, avoid asking solely informational questions that do not contribute to advancing the negotiation.
When the seller emphasizes the value and quality of the product, avoid making significantly lower offers that may signal lack of confidence and weaken your bargaining position.
When the buyer references a newer model at a lower price to justify a discount, you should consider adjusting your price accordingly to secure the sale.

When the seller confirms the item's good condition matching the buyer's description, avoid reiterating details without indicating price flexibility to prevent weakening the buyer's position in negotiations.

When the seller indicates dissatisfaction and requests a higher counteroffer, avoid proposing a price lower than your own initial reference price, as it may weaken your leverage and allow the seller to push for a higher amount.

When the seller emphasizes the item's excellent condition and accessories, avoid increasing your offer by small increments as it may weaken your leverage and allow the seller to push for a higher final price.
When the seller agrees to a price close to the buyer's maximum limit, you should clearly state your final offer to secure a favorable deal.
When the seller has already accepted the buyer's offer, avoid making unnecessary closing statements like 'Thank you!' to prevent any potential ambiguity or confusion in the negotiation process.
When the seller indicates openness to your price and offers options to consider, avoid merely confirming plans without advancing the price negotiation or introducing new concessions.
When the seller states a firm price but shows willingness to negotiate with incentives, you should introduce payment urgency and flexible payment methods to encourage immediate concessions.
When the seller has clearly stated a minimum acceptable price, avoid making offers significantly below that minimum as it can harden the seller's stance and reduce your negotiation leverage.
When the seller maintains a firm price based on item condition and ownership history, you should introduce a competitive external alternative to create leverage and encourage a price reduction.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate and signals personal rapport, you should make a firm, immediate offer to create urgency and encourage final concession.
When the seller responds to a very low offer with minimal concession, you should assert your price firmly to establish a strong anchor and encourage incremental movement in the negotiation.
When the seller has set a high initial price but shows willingness to negotiate, you should politely request a price reduction to encourage an immediate concession and advance the negotiation.
When the seller signals willingness to negotiate but rejects a low initial offer, avoid making an aggressive lowball offer that may provoke a higher counteroffer and reduce your leverage.
When the seller makes a counteroffer including valuable features, you should clarify the terms to confirm added value without conceding on price.
When the seller confidently assures product durability in response to concerns, avoid raising objections without coupling them with specific price or concession requests.

When the seller explains a product flaw as caused by an external accident rather than product quality, you should use this to highlight potential condition issues and justify negotiating a lower price.
When the seller acknowledges the value of the item and shows openness to negotiation, you should demonstrate flexibility by increasing your offer strategically to reach a mutually acceptable price.
When the seller has accepted your offer, avoid making non-substantive acknowledgments that do not advance the negotiation or improve the deal.
When the seller confirms the item is in excellent condition but expresses willingness to negotiate, you should ask detailed questions about the item's state to open negotiation opportunities.
When the seller expresses willingness to negotiate price, you should make a clear, low initial offer to create leverage and prompt a significant price reduction.
When the seller makes a counteroffer below their initial price, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.

When the seller reaffirms the product’s value and insists on the asking price without concessions, avoid providing only contextual or clarifying information without addressing price or making a counteroffer.
When the seller proposes a firm price with a delivery condition, you should anchor your offer at your target price while offering a convenient meeting point to encourage seller concession.
When the seller offers a counterprice between the initial offers, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.
When the seller has already disclosed included accessories and their condition, avoid asking redundant questions that do not create new leverage or directly influence price concessions.
When the seller confirms ownership and item authenticity without adjusting price, avoid asking questions that do not directly advance the negotiation or justify a price change.
When the seller has made a counteroffer above the buyer's initial offer, avoid immediately accepting the higher price without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage.

When the seller emphasizes product quality and confirms fixed product attributes without discussing price, avoid asking questions unrelated to price negotiation that do not create leverage to lower the price.
When the seller provides a vague or non-specific answer about product warranty duration, avoid relying solely on that information to justify a price increase or to concede in negotiation.

When the seller responds with a counteroffer lower than their initial price after the buyer explicitly states a maximum offer and willingness to negotiate, you should present a clear target price to anchor the negotiation and prompt concessions.

When the seller reiterates product value and adjusts the price slightly without acknowledging buyer concessions, avoid repeating your initial offer without adding new incentives or addressing seller concerns.
When the seller maintains a firm price but shows willingness to negotiate, you should make a small concession to signal flexibility and encourage the seller to lower their price further.
When the seller emphasizes the high value and market price of the item, avoid making offers that are significantly below both the seller's price and the item's perceived worth.

When the seller maintains a high price by emphasizing added value, avoid making small incremental price increases that reduce your leverage without sufficiently pressuring the seller to lower their price.
When the seller acknowledges that the buyer has found cheaper alternatives, you should challenge the seller's price competitiveness to prompt them to invite your best offer.
When the seller invites your best price, avoid significantly lowering your own maximum offer as it weakens your leverage and encourages the seller to raise their counteroffer.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer close to your maximum, you should propose a compromise price between your offer and theirs to facilitate agreement and secure a better deal.
When the seller has already accepted a negotiated price, avoid making redundant acknowledgments that do not advance the negotiation or improve terms.
When the seller emphasizes added value items to justify a higher price, you should remove or decline those items to weaken their justification and encourage a price reduction.
When the seller has lowered their price after removing extras, avoid making a drastically lower offer that undermines your credibility and reduces your leverage in the negotiation.
When the seller firmly sets a minimum acceptable price, you should make a reasonable counteroffer that narrows the gap to demonstrate flexibility and encourage further concessions.
When the seller firmly states a minimum acceptable price, avoid immediately conceding to that price with added conditions that do not lower the price, as it weakens your negotiation leverage.
When the seller indicates limited price flexibility while emphasizing product value, avoid vague or non-committal inquiries about price without proposing a specific offer or concession.
When the seller justifies a higher price by including additional items, you should explicitly decline those extras to negotiate a lower base price.
When the seller has made a partial price concession but maintains a firm stance, you should propose a lower target price to pressure the seller into further reducing their offer.
When the seller has made a firm but negotiable counteroffer, you should present a concrete, slightly improved offer with added incentives like immediate payment or pickup to encourage agreement.
